speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Wenman (Fraser Valley West) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR POWER STATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider declaring a moratorium on the further construction of nuclear power stations pending the report of a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons to look into ways and means of improving techniques for radioactive waste disposal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a number of years ago some other members of the House of Commons and I had an opportunity to examine closely Canada's nuclear industry through questioning in the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. I remember at the time, in late 1977, the then minister of energy, mines and resources, Hon. Alastair Gillespie, stating with very strong confidence to myself and my colleagues that the answer to the problem of nuclear waste
Radioactive Waste Disposal
disposal was at hand. Perhaps he could be forgiven for his remarks since he was using the report of Dr. Hare as his source, which indicated in 1977 that "there are good prospects for the safe, permanent disposal of reactor wastes and irradiated fuel." Unfortunately, three years have passed since those remarks were made and the Hare report was published, and we are no closer to a solution today than we were at that time.
The most recent study of the problem by an all-party committee of the Ontario legislature made some interesting conclusions, specifically that Canada's nuclear waste program is ineffective, run by the wrong organization and foundering on public mistrust. The committee found fault with both federal and provincial governments for a lack of adequate research into disposal sites and a failure to support stringent safety regulations when shipping radioactive materials. Moreover, the committee concluded that governments have tended to present biased accounts to the public in regard to nuclear fuel disposal.
I believe the remarks of the minister to which I referred earlier are an example of such biased, overly optimistic accounts.
I almost wish the former member for Etobicoke were here with us today to give us further reassuring testimony. Instead, we must now face the reality of nuclear wastes without the comfort of even his verbal safeguards which have become unfounded over the past three years. What happened to the "good prospects" referred to in the Hare report? Nuclear wastes pose a threat to the environment, and subsequently are a threat to the health and safety of all of us and our constituents. The danger of these wastes is a function of the extreme radioactivity of spent fuel of any nuclear reactor. For several reasons the most significant of these waste products is plutonium-239, known in some circles as the "element of the lord of hell". Although primarily known and feared as the principal component of atomic weaponry, plutonium-239 also is the central threat to our environment. It is known that one milligram of this element can cause lung cancer if inhaled. In laboratory tests one eight-millionth of a pound of plutonium-239 caused lung cancer in animals. In fact it is one of the most lethal poisons known to mankind.
Compounding the lethality problem of plutonium is the incredible longevity of the element. Whereas other reactor waste products may have a half life in the order of 30 years, that of plutonium-239 in fact is 24,000 years, that is, fully one half of all the plutonium-239 we produce today will still be with us with its attendant radioactivity 24,000 years from now. Expressed in other terms, it will take 240,000 years before the plutonium-239 created today will reach a low enough level of radioactivity to present no real threat to the human race or our environment. Nor is plutonium-239 the only radioactive waste product of nuclear reactors.
Even the heavy water used as a moderator in the Candu emerges from the reactor radioactive, and all radioactivity affects human tissue in exactly the same way. By ionizing atoms it changes the configuration of cellular molecules. In so far as molecular function depends upon its configuration, that molecule, and hence the cell, becomes incapable of fulfilling its intended function. It has been found that radium which is

October 20, 1980
Radioactive Waste Disposal
similar to plutonium-239 in its effects on the human body can cause necrosis and tumours of the bone and anaemia resulting in death. Also it can result in cancer of the skin, lungs and thyroid.
I have dwelt for some time on the unpleasant details of radioactivity because it is important for all members of the House to realize the consequences of plunging headlong into the development of nuclear power. I say "headlong" because the government has yet to provide any clear indication of progress in regard to the problem of waste management. I should have excited the minister, but I have been unable to. But, 1 have cited the example of a minister's responsibility for overseeing the development of a Canadian nuclear policy over the last few years. He said that solution was at hand, that in fact they had found the solution. They have not found the solution. I defy anyone in the nuclear industry to come forward now and state that we are closer to a solution than we were in 1977. I hope in response to this motion today that someone will stand and say if there is any such person. I hope that person will come forward and state that we are closer to a solution than we were in 1977. Any reading of science I have done indicates that in fact we are no closer.
1 understand that AECL has now delayed for at least two years the selection of a disposal site for Canada's nuclear wastes, so three years is extended to five years. Let me give an example of the consequences of the failure to find such a disposal site. In my own riding I have been trying for the last four years to have some low-level radioactive material removed from a specific site in Surrey. Earlier AECB made a commitment to remove the material by December of this year. I am afraid that kind of commitment is like the one given by the former minister who said that a waste site would be found for high-level radioactive wastes. We cannot even solve the basic problem of low-level radioactive waste. Now they are saying that this December guarantee to remove this product from my riding to a more permanent waste disposal site may not be met. And it is now suddenly up to the provinces. Now that we cannot find a solution, throw it to the provinces, which seems to be the policy of the federal government.
[DOT] <mo)
I think in this particular case we have a clear example of the irresponsible behaviour of the present government and its agencies in regard to nuclear energy and radioactive waste disposal. The AECB in this case licensed the manufacturing process which created radioactive wastes, yet once the wastes were left behind the AECB refused to accept responsibility for them, sloughing them off instead onto the provincial government.
It is this kind of attitude which contributes to public contempt and suspicion of the nuclear industry in Canada. A Gallup poll taken January 11 of this year, commissioned by none other than the AECL themselves, found that 47 per cent of Ontario residents opposed a waste disposal site in their community, even if a safe disposal method were found, while 39 per cent did not know, and only 6 per cent supported the
idea of a waste disposal site. There has to be a reason why these people are concerned. 1 have listened to some of these reasons for their concern and I cannot understand why the government opposite is not concerned in the same way.
There is good reason to oppose a nuclear waste disposal site in your community. In the first place a satisfactory storage system has yet to be worked out. Immobilizing the waste in glass has been suggested, but unless an adequate cooling system can be developed the glass itself will melt down and leak wastes into the soil. Furthermore, the reacting waste forms gases which could shatter the glass unit. Other problems relate to the site itself. Drilling holes into granite creates fractures, these fractures in turn might allow the entry of water. Earthquake activity can further extend a fracture. We must never forget that we are dealing not with decades, or more centuries, but with thousands upon thousands of years. These are some of the problems which have to be faced. We should not deceive ourselves into thinking the problem is an insignificant one.
Right now the only means we have for looking after radioactive wastes is to store them in temporary cooling ponds, which are a type of large swimming pool. Every day 1700 pounds of reactor wastes are placed in these pools from Ontario's reactors alone. By the year 2,000 we will have to find a way of disposing of 80,000 tons of highly radioactive waste. In this context I should point out that these statistics come from the commission's report itself entitled "The Management of Canada's Nuclear Wastes." The report recommended a step-by-step program calling for an operating repository capable of receiving Canada's nuclear wastes to be in operation by 1995 to 2,000. We have yet to reach the first step in that program, which was the declaration of a national plan to deal with nuclear wastes. Is that the kind of response we are going to get? The prospect of 80,000 tons of radioactive waste sitting around in storage pools becomes increasingly unpleasant.
At this point a most obvious question springs to mind. Canada's first nuclear reactor started up in 1945 when this country was, and is, foremost in nuclear energy research. We were leaders, and perhaps we still are, in nuclear technology, but we are not leaders in the disposal of the waste products from our technology. There is absolutely no excuse for a country as technologically developed as Canada to have made no provisions for the management of reactor wastes. Yet despite the fact Canada's commercial nuclear program has been in operation since 1962, the minister of the environment, when I questioned him in committee in 1976, referred to the disposal of nuclear wastes as a "new development". His deputy minister then elaborated by saying that the Department of the Environment and the Department of Energy had recently been contacted to pursue the matter and to come up with policy recommendations.
Sixteen years passed after the first commercial reactor started before the government realized it had a problem on its hands with the storage and disposal of nuclear wastes. Granted, a reactor usually takes ten years before it is producing significant amounts of waste. But we have not stopped at just
October 20, 1980

one reactor, we have continued to build more, with little or no regard for environmental consequences.
This leads me to another point. Not only have we continued to construct nuclear reactors without having any means of disposing of the wastes. Moreover, we have exported our nuclear technology and its incumbent problems to any country willing to pay the price. We have exported the technology, we have exported the basic raw materials, but we have not been able to provide the expertise to deal with the disposal of the wastes. Here we enter into the realm of safeguards and a whole host of other complications to this industry. India constructed her first nuclear explosive device with the aid of a Candu reactor. Pakistan is well on its way to producing an atomic bomb. But those very real problems tend to obscure another aspect of nuclear sales and one which becomes increasingly more significant for those countries with peaceful intentions. I am referring specifically to the problem of waste disposal for those countries which accept this bargain of unlimited energy in exchange for the hazards of nuclear wastes.
I refer again to my questioning of cabinet ministers in 1976. I asked if Canada has a moral obligation, a moral responsibility. If we are going to export this technology, these raw materials to less developed countries than ourselves when we cannot handle the wastes, how do we expect them to do so? The then minister of the environment replied that he could not do anything about that because he did not have the information to give them. Therefore, it stands that if we cannot provide the information to help nations protect themselves from our technology, are we not morally obligated not to export it?
Furthermore, the minister said the Canadian government had no means of implementing in other countries the environmental rules we may observe in our own country. That position was confirmed by the minister then responsible for external affairs. Given this attitude, which has not changed in the four years since those statements were made, it is clear the government is guilty of moral bankruptcy for continuing to export our nuclear capabilities to countries less equipped than ourselves to handle these potentially dangerous problems. It is equally clear the government should cease to export any nuclear materials until such time as adequate safety and environmental standards are in effect. If need be, this would include the return to Canada of all spent fuels from our nuclear reactors abroad. But of course we cannot do that because we have no means of dealing with the transportation or handling of these wastes once they have reached our shores.
The previous government was prepared to face the problems posed by nuclear energy. The Conservative party had indicated its intention and had begun to establish a joint House and Senate committee to examine the various aspects of nuclear power. My own motion, which I sponsor here today, is more modest in its scope in that it calls for an examination of the nuclear waste problem only. However, it is because of the long term and significant dangers associated with spent fuels that I ask the House today to consider placing a moratorium on the
Radioactive Waste Disposal
future construction of nuclear power plants until the problem of wastes can be adequately dealt with. I am not saying we have to stop our industry, 1 am saying we have to spend as much energy finding solutions to the problem of nuclear waste as we spend paying bribes to foreign governments to buy our technology. If we spent just that much effort perhaps we would get closer to that solution which is supposedly at hand.
This issue is still too important to be left to internal departmental study, which is a very convenient way of putting something on the shelf and forgetting about it. It demands attention from members of all parties of this House of Commons. Because of the threat posed by nuclear wastes to future generations, this House would be derelict in its responsibility to the Canadian people if it did not hold public hearings. Why should the public not have its say in this country as it does in almost every country in the world?
It is clear that attempts to advance waste disposal research further are hampered by a public distrust of AECL. It is equally clear that such distrust is, to a large extent, justified. AECL continues to see waste disposal as a public relations problem. Combined with the failure to do anything about nuclear waste until the problem is almost unmanageable, AECL's attitude has alienated those very people whom it can least afford to offend. Public hearings by a joint House-Senate committee would enable both sides to clear the air and would be considerably less partisan than an industry-sponsored hearing which must consider its own vested interest. This is a matter for government, not a matter for the industry.
I would like to sum up with a brief thought. In the case of plutonium-239, in the words of an author of a recent book on this subject, "We are asking all foreseeable generations of human beings to guard this element from accident, sabotage and acts of God". The very least we can do as responsible members of Parliament is to try to ensure that from the moment we knew about the problem, from that very moment, we began with all our efforts to seek solutions, knowledge and technology relative to waste disposal so that we can safeguard, not just ourselves, but future generations of not only Canadians, but mankind.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR POWER STATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the initiative taken by the hon. member opposite in raising the question of nuclear matters in Canada today, particularly the question of nuclear-spent fuel disposal and the related matter of public participation in that important subject.
The hon. member has drawn to the attention of the House the fact that the generation of electricity by nuclear reactors carries with it the problem of how we can best dispose safely of the spent fuel produced.
More than 99 per cent of the radioactive material produced in the typical Candu station remains in the used fuel which is now stored temporarily at the reactor sites. Hon. members will be aware that this fuel contains useful material which could be

October 20, 1980
Radioactive Waste Disposal
recovered and used to produce yet more energy as technology to that end develops. If the useful material were to be recycled, most of the residual radioactive material would be left behind as separated waste. No matter whether the radioactive material is left in the fuel or separated as waste, clearly, as the hon. member opposite pointed out, it must be handled with care and isolated from man until the radioactivity decreases to an insignificant level.
The question then arises as to whether this can be done safely. We have heard today of the present practice which is to store the spent fuel at the reactor sites. It can indeed be stored there indefinitely with suitable maintenance, but that practice would place a burden on future generations, to maintain that high degree of surveillance over the spent fuel. Accordingly, researchers are working, under agreement reached between the Ontario government and the national government, to investigate various ways of permanent disposal. The choice to be made is to discard the entire used fuel bundles from the reactors after sealing them in corrosion-proof containers, in which case the used fuel would be considered a waste in the true sense of the word, or to recycle the useful materials in the used fuel and melt the pure wastes, that is the fission byproducts, together with glass-making chemicals to produce a highly insoluble solid for disposal. Scientists and engineers, including the geologists, involved in this research agree on the suitability of geological disposal. The used fuel or solid radioactive glass waste would be placed in a deep vault carved out of primeval rock.
In Canada we are fortunate in that we have, for example, in the Canadian Shield more than 1,000 locations which have the theoretical potential as sites for waste disposal. A nuclear waste vault in such circumstances would look like a large hard rock mine with the spent fuel isolated under 500 to 1,000 metres of rock. A single vault would be sufficient to hold all of the nuclear waste produced in Canada for the next 50 years.
That research which, as I say, has been conducted under the aegis of the Ontraio government and the federal government, has been subjected to a variety of reviews. In a few minutes I want to turn to the question raised by the hon. member on public participation in this aspect as well as other aspects of nuclear energy generation. Before doing so, however, I want to refer to the annual report of the technical advisory committee on nuclear fuel waste management program, a committee of independent experts, of which the hon. member opposite may know.
It might be useful if I were to point out to the House that in the committee's over-all view, the current research program is well conceived. There are many impressive accomplishments, as the report of the technical advisory committee notes, and the research objectives are becoming more clearly defined and the most critical areas in which more research is needed are being identified. The committee was reassured by the increasing participation in the program by university and industry scientists and engineers and the excellent understanding of relevant international research activities on the part of the principal investigators.
The committee in its report in May stressed that a proper scientific and technical evaluation of the program can only be made if the necessary research information is available. In particular it noted that extensive geoscientific work in the field is necessary and that it is essential that approvals for field research be obtained. I might add parenthetically that such activity is going forward at this very moment.
Further, the committee affirmed its general approval and support for major increases in funding for the expansion of the geoscientific and geotechnical programs, especially in regard to field research activities and the development of an underground research laboratory.
In discussing the work which has been done in the field of evaluation of the current program for the disposal of nuclear spent fuel, the hon. member opposite made reference to the final report of the select committee on Ontario hydro affairs of the Ontario legislature. I am pleased that he did so because that report contains much information of value to those who are actively concerned with the current research phase of the spent fuel program.
The hon. member opposite may be aware that the report of the Ontario select committee has characterized the current nuclear waste program as fundamentally sound. It has also put forward a number of proposals for futher evolution in the current practices in the program, practices mainly related to the participation of the public and to the over-all management of the program. I can assure the hon. member that those recommendations will be studied by the federal government as well as by the Ontario government. I am quite certain that many of them will be subjects of discussion between the two levels of government.
I see that the time is passing. The hon. member opposite, in bringing forward his motion, has raised a variety of subjects to which I would like to respond. However, given the limited time available, it might be better if I were to restrict myself to one or two of his observations.
He spoke of the problems associated with the export of nuclear technology from Canada. First he drew a picture of his concern about the safeguards which are in place to prevent any repetition of the experience with India and to prevent the abuse of Candu technology by countries importing that technology. I am sure the hon. member is aware that the Canadian safeguard provisions against non-proliferation are as stringent and as demanding as any in the world today. 1 am sure he is very conscious that Canada has foregone commercial opportunities for additional commercial sales as a result of our commitment to an unparalleled high level of safeguards against nuclear proliferation.

speechtext:
Second, in terms of technology with regard to spent fuel disposal, the hon. member opposite will be aware that the Canadian research program is merely one of many such programs. Many research programs are conducted by
October 20, 1980

other governments which generate electricity through nuclear fission. Additionally there are, of course, international research programs under the aegis of the International Atomic Energy Authority in Vienna. Those programs of research are also directed toward some of the questions which the hon. member opposite raised earlier.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us calls for a moratorium on the further construction of nuclear power stations. 1 do not know whether the hon. member had that moratorium in mind for Canada only or whether he also meant a prohibition on the export of nuclear technology. Be that as it may, he looks for a moratorium while improved techniques for radioactive waste disposal would be examined by a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
In our view a moratorium might be appropriate in areas where the government cannot proceed because of confusion or indecision. I do not know whether it was that experience of the previous government in this area which led it to the proposal for a moratorium when it was in office. For our part, we have not felt the need for a moratorium because our policy is not marked by confusion or indecision. On the contrary, the government's views on nuclear energy, and particularly on the future of the nuclear industry in Canada, were set forth in a brief statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as reported in Hansard for May 1, 1980. The Prime Minister said we were not undertaking a public inquiry, in the broad sense of the word, because we believed the time schedule for keeping our nuclear industry viable is short. The Prime Minister also noted that we were in some danger of seeing the Canadian nuclear industry become obsolete and losing its opportunities to sell Canadian high technology in other countries. He noted too that we wanted to take this opportunity to determine in what ways the promotion of the Canadian nuclear industry and, indeed, the sales abroad of Candu technology, might be encouraged. There is no intention, of course, in that connection to prevent the Canadian public, either concurrently with the review or subsequently, from expressing their views. The Prime Minister did stress that a long inquiry about whether, as he put it, we stay in the game or get out, would not be feasible since it might well be during the time taken up by such an inquiry that our industry lost its momentum in the face of both international competition and national considerations.
Mr. Speaker, as members of the House know, there have been a variety of inquiries here in Canada over recent years into the various aspects of the generation of nuclear energy. I would refer the hon. member opposite, when he raises the question how Canadians have had such opportunities, to a whole series of inquiries. I might mention the Cluff Lake board of inquiry in Saskatchewan, the Ontario Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning, the Ontario Royal Commission on the Health and Safety of Workers in the Mines, the Select Committee of the Ontario Legislature investigating Ontario Hydro affairs-to which the hon. member referred- the Ontario Environmental Assessment Board into the expansion of the uranium mines in the Elliot Lake area, the Federal
Radioactive Waste Disposal
Environmental Assessment Review Office panels on Eldorado's proposed uranium refineries, and meetings of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works of the House which has addressed a variety of nuclear energy questions. I should add, of course, that members may have available the first report of the technical advisory committee on the nuclear fuel waste management program, to which I referred earlier. I am sure the hon. member opposite, coming from British Columbia, will be aware of the Bates inquiry which is finishing its work. There is also a provincial parliamentary committee which has been looking into various questions relating to nuclear generation in New Brunswick.
With such a variety of reports, commissions, inquiries and boards in place over recent years, there has not, in our view, been any lack of opportunity for public participation in the discussion of nuclear energy questions.
In addition, both the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and I myself in recent months have had an opportunity to meet with representatives of a variety of organizations, some representing the nuclear industry and others representing such bodies as Energy Probe, Energy Pathways and the Canadian Coalition for Nuclear Responsibility, which represent a range of attitudes towards nuclear energy. We have had the benefit of their views and so have the public servants involved in the current review of the nuclear industry.
In raising questions about the nuclear energy industry in Canada I would have thought the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) might have spent a moment or two more on the various benefits which have accrued to Canadians from that energy option of which he is so much aware. I am sure it was only through lack of time that he did not. There are, in my view, three principal ways and a number of subsidiary ways in which the nuclear energy industry in Canada is of benefit to Canadians.
It is important, first, as an essential part of our diversified energy strategy. Second, the Candu reactor is a leader in Canadian industrial development in the high technology area. The Candu industry is one of the few industries of wholly Canadian character with a high degree of technological content. As many international observers have pointed out, the Candu reactor is a remarkable achievement in an area of great technical challenge.
Third, the Candu industry, in its export potential, represents a vehicle to help carry Canadian industries into foreign markets and to bring the benefits of Canadian technology to countries which are desperately short of energy and which can find through nuclear generation the sources of energy for their industry and domestic use which they so much need.
I believe my time is about up, although I could add more about the nature of the nuclear industry in Canada.

Radioactive Waste Disposal

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED MORATORIUM ON CONSTRUCTION OF NUCLEAR POWER STATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to support the motion put forward by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), although 1 must say I do not think it goes far enough either in dealing with a moratorium on the waste disposal problem or in dealing with the industry itself. Having listened to the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, one is left with the feeling that should the waste disposal problem be dealt with adequately he would certainly be supporting the nuclear industry. The previous speaker made some comments in relation to the value of the nuclear industry to the Canadian economy, but I did not hear him or any other member of his party propose their ridings as a national disposal site for waste in Canada.
Looking at the field as a whole, there are five main areas which need to be dealt with. The first is mining, the impact the actual removal of uranium from the ground and the primary milling processes will have on the workers in that area, along with the storage of first-level refined ore. This is an area where very little money has been spent by the federal government in assessing the health impact and the environmental impact, though both are very real and tragic.
The second relates to refining. Some money has been spent on this. The main expenditures have been on fuel fabrication and the fuel cycle itself, the actual phase whereby some cash flow is generated. The government has been spending money in this specific area.
The problem of waste disposal is one that disturbs not only myself but people everywhere because of the dramatic expansion in the volume of nuclear wastes sitting in various places around the world. It is interesting to look at a recent energy, mines and resources report which points out some of the factors they are considering. Most members of this House are aware that most of the fuel bundles and wastes from the nuclear cycle have been stored in cooled-water areas. This is called surface disposal. One of the less enlightened proposals which have been discussed involves sticking the nuclear waste into the Arctic or Antarctic ice sheets, which all of us know are likely to melt at some point, certainly with the "greenhouse effect" from C02 that is now affecting the world.
Disposal into outer space is another very unenlightened proposal. Disposal on ocean plains is another option the United States and a number of European countries are now considering, though with some distaste, because when this method was used in the past the containers burst open releasing nuclear waste. Frequently overlooked in connection with this type of disposal method, is the fact that once the nuclear waste gets into the environment, it is very quickly bio-accumulated, rising up the food chain and into the food web and eventually into man, who is at the top of the food chain.
Another prospect is geological containment on land, a method that seems to be preferred by members opposite. 1 will be raising some very serious questions this afternoon regarding that proposal, including the use of salt formations for disposal purposes.
Last year 1 had the opportunity to ask some questions of the vice-president of research for Atomic Energy of Canada, Mr. Hart. I would like to put a couple of his responses on the record. 1 asked him:
-first, where waste is at present being stored in Canada; how much, in gross tonnage; and exactly how it gets there from the site it is currently at.
Mr. Hart replied:
I do not have the exact tonnage, but you can think of it as about one Olympic-size swimming pool, perhaps half to two-thirds full.
In my view, that is a pretty frivolous attitude to take toward a very serious environmental problem, one that we all recognize as capable of causing serious cancers in man. The second question I put is very relevant to the proposals put forward from the government side regarding geological containment on land. 1 put the following question to Mr. Hart at that time:
If we look, for example, at the Atikokan and Sudbury areas, if the waste was to be moved from one site to another, could you give us some idea of how that waste would be moved there? Also, in what form is it going to be stored in the geological areas that it is proposed to place it in?
Mr. Hart replied:
If a site is selected away from the reactors, which is likely, the fuel will be transported in shielded flasks which have been tested for fire resistance, crash resistance; there are some other tests as well. It will be transported either by road or rail and taken to the site. When it is at the site, the concept we have now, which is still, as I say, under research, is that it will be buried deep in a stable geologic formation. The material will, in fact, be buried deep in these formations. It will be tested for some time in that formation and then the hole will be backfilled. It will be monitored for a while, but the idea is to prove that it can be left unattended for all time.
It is important to point out some of the problems of locking it into geological containment. For example, ground water could at some future point get in and move some of the radioactive materials into the ground water supply. Members opposite, and perhaps those to my right, should become better versed about such things as iodine 129. The half life of iodine 129 is 17 million years. When we are talking about that type of containment or some of these other government proposals, such as placing it in the ocean or in ice sheets, we are talking about geological time. We are simply not talking about the history of civilization, which extends for only 10,000 years. We are talking about the safe disposal of wastes that have many millions of years in just half lives. There could be further ice ages, enormous disruptions on the planet; the placement of materials of this type in the environment in any way at this point in time is inadvisable. At some future date another generation will have to pay for the risk we took in order to better our lives. We have not really reflected on the very serious health dangers our actions will impose on future generations.
Another example is technetium 99, again a substance with a multimillion-year half life, capable of moving very quickly in the groundwater system. This is something we should keep very much in mind. Very pertinent to our discussion today is another question I put to Mr. Hart last year. I quote:
Exactly how radioactive is the material that would be moved? For example, if the container were here in the room and there was a crash and some of it fell out on the floor, just how radioactive is it?

The flasks have been tested by a railway locomotive going 80 miles an hour crashing into a solid concrete abutment, and there was, in fact, no leakage at all.

1 question the intelligence of our friendly scientists working for Atomic Energy who would think of such an experiment as tying a flask on the front of a locomotive and running the locomotive into a cement wall at 80 miles an hour. Some pretty serious questions concerning responsibilities to the Canadian public arise when a statement like that is put on the record. Ele went on to say:
You could sit on the flask itself. If there was some leakage, I guess it would depend on how much.
1 think that is self-evident, Mr. Speaker. The exchange goes on as follows:

speechtext:
Let us say there was a pound of it here in the middle of the floor.
Hon. members should keep in mind that if there were a pound of this material from one of the nuclear plants in Canada sitting on the floor of this chamber, I would be equally anxious to ask the vice-president in charge of research whether I would be safe sitting here. He replied:
If there was a pound of it in the middle of the floor, no, you probably would not be safe sitting here. You would probably be safe sitting back at the door there.
I really question what is happening in the nuclear industry in Canada when we get such statements from people who are being paid by the taxpayers of this country and, who go to such lengths as tying a flask of radioactive material on the front of a locomotive and then running that locomotive into a wall at 80 miles an hour! If that is government policy, then I think we have a much more serious question on our hands than perhaps immediately meets the eye.
It is not only the waste from the nuclear industry itself which causes problems; there are radioactive wastes from industry as well. A lot of people do not recognize that smoke detectors, for instance, contain radioactive material. Hospitals and universities also house such material. Earlier in this session I raised a question in the House regarding the University of British Columbia. It is my understanding that over the last couple of decades the university has simply dumped its radioactive waste in Vancouver Harbour, off Point Atkinson. Apparently someone went out in a rowboat and simply threw it over the side. I have gone to a great deal of trouble to try to find out where the waste sites are but officials do not recall where the radioactive waste was dumped from the boats.
This is not an unfamiliar problem, Mr. Speaker. Quite recently questions were put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in this House regarding the transportation of radioactive material in Canada. It appears that when 58 containers of ore were being moved on a passenger flight in this country, not one of them had the lid properly secured.
We have to look not only at the health of workers in the mining industry but also at refining, fuel fabrication and the fuel cycle to see the dangers to the public and workers. The majority of funds in this country are going to those two areas, which are highly scientific and highly technical.
Radioactive Waste Disposal
A few days ago in Toronto I had the opportunity of listening to Dr. Noel Brown, Chairman of the United Nations Environment Planning Committee who gave a very interesting overview of the Three Mile Island incident. He pointed out that had that incident occurred anywhere else in the world-for example in places where our CAN DU reactors have gone-it might not have been so easily dealt with. In the United States, and to a great extent in Canada, there are enough scientists in the nuclear field who could get together quickly in an emergency. But had such a thing happened in India, for example, there might have been a much more serious incident because of the lack of an adequate scientific response.
I must point out that the hesitant, piecemeal approach which has marked the entire history of the nuclear industry, going back to the 1930s was taken because of sheer economic expediency. In all our efforts to get a saleable commodity, be it electricity or the various readioactive substances used in medicine, sheer economic expediency has governed our dealings with health or environmental issues. Very little money has been spent on these very serious problems and we have yet to hear from the government of any major new expenditures in this regard.
I should like to return to the prospect of placing these containers, be they composed of cement or of various metals, whatever the scientific community decides, in the geological formations. How long will it be before the various radionuclides reach the surface? That is a serious question, since it is inevitable that they will. All the types of storage tried to date have been viable at the very best in terms of centuries. These materials will inevitably get back to the surface. They will work their way into streams and back to the food web and thus have a very serious impact on man.
A case in point is Eldorado Nuclear Ltd. which is still dumping waste at Port Granby. At this time, all levels of government are co-operating to try to get that company to expand-particularly its uranium hexafluoride operation, commonly known as UF6-from 5,000 metric tons per year to
9,000	by 1984. The nuclear garbage coming from that industry will be around, not for decades or centuries, but for ice ages to come, so we must be concerned about the impact of such debris on future generations.
As recently as 1976, $7 million was allocated to clean up Port Hope where 550 homes were found to have radiation levels above AECB health standards. I think most hon. members have a fairly good understanding of the Love Canal incident in the United Sates, of which there are now potentially hundreds. We have Canada's very own, home-grown Love Canal situations as a result of a government which did not care to allocate enough money to make sure things were done right from the very beginning and that conditions were made safe. So far, building materials including studs and parts of walls have been removed from 220 homes that contained the highest levels of radioactivity. A further 152 homes have had stacks installed in order to remove loose radon gas from them. I must point out that radon gas has had a very serious impact on the health of workers in the uranium industry and that very little

research is being done on the problem. Soil has been removed from beneath 280 homes sites because the ore left over from the refining process was highly radioactive. 200,000	tons of contaminated earth in Port Hope. I am not aware that the government has any plans to deal with this serious situation.
1 should like to quote a statement of George Wald, the 1967 Nobel Prize winner as follows:
-no one knows how to store the waste products, which will remain dangerous for half a million years. The whole of human civilization is perhaps 10,000 years old, and we are producing material that will represent a lethal liability for man and for life on earth for hundreds of thousands of years to come. subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when 1 was speaking at five o'clock, I was expressing the opinion that confederation has been a remarkable success. 1 talked very briefly about our economic system which has evolved and which combines the best of the free enterprise system and social obligations to the less fortunate and our dedication to the quality of life, thus providing our system with the best educated work force in the world and the healthiest population because of medicare.
October 20, 1980

I spoke of our equalization principle. Without it there could be no equality of opportunity in this country. I spoke about the principle that those who can afford it should help those in need, not only on an individual basis through the transfer of unemployment insurance, for example, from the worker in Ontario to those less fortunate, but also with the transfer of funds through our equalization formula.
Canada has been a remarkable success story, and it is recognized around the world that we have the finest country in the world. When we combine our standard of living with our degree of freedoms, 1 doubt if any country can match ours.
However, if confederation has been such a great success, why am I an advocate of the proposed resolution before the House, which in a relatively short period of time I hope will be referred to the special joint committee of the House and the Senate? As learned members opposite have emphasized in the last week, the fundamental philosophy behind the BNA Act has been, of course, compromise. It reflects a combination of the civil code, for instance, and jurisprudence to look after the rights of individuals.
But the one defect and the main defect in the BNA Act, is that it does not contain an amending formula. It does not contain an amending formula because the Fathers of Confederation did not think one was necessary. Perhaps in the light of the times one was not necessary. Forceful advocates of the rights of English Catholics like Connolly and McGee made sure that our rights were protected in the BNA Act. Others made sure that the rights of English Protestants were protected under section 133. Concern for French-speaking Canadians in the west was minimal. Numerically it was not a problem. Even the rights of French-speaking Canadians in Ontario were not a pressing problem in the field of education, because where French-speaking Ontarians lived they lived together and could control their own system of education and their own schools that long ago.
There is a relationship between the concern of Canadians today for individual rights ard the general acceptance across Canada at this very moment today that we should get on with the business at hand, that this proposed resolution should be debated a few more days and then sent on to committee. I think this is the first time since I came here in 1962 that Canadians have shown any concern at all about the issue of constitutional change. If anything, the tendency in the past has been to say, "Oh, not again; why are you debating proposed constitutional changes and amending formulae at a time when we have unemployment problems, inflation problems, tariff problems and energy policy problems?" I think the reason is that in recent years Canadians have become more conscious of individual rights and of how fragile individual rights really are.
Our history has been blemished like the history of any other country, and I will not repeat what has been said in this House about how we treated Canadians of Japanese origin during the war, about how we treated the Jehovah's Witnesses in Quebec in the 1950s and the infamous padlock law, about how some of the privileges of English-speaking Quebeckers have been eradicated, the result of provincial legislation, and about how in
The Constitution
most provinces in this country individual rights of people, particularly in the field of education, are not as generous as they were at the time of confederation. This is unfortunate, but I think that perhaps for the first time the need to enshrine our rights in the constitution has become a real issue in many homes.
Take, for instance, the whole issue of mobility. I was minister of labour for a number of years, close to the labour movement as a result, and 1 can remember the anger, the agony of trade unions in this country, particularly in the construction industry, when construction workers in Cornwall found they could not work in the province of Quebec two years ago, and when painters from Hull could not work in the national capital, in Ottawa. This was a real issue which was resolved through debate and discussion between appropriate ministers of one province and the other, but the element of retaliation was there: "If you do not allow our construction workers in your province, we will not allow your painters in our province." This registered with Canadians, particularly those who come from Europe.
I can remember one very angry union leader asking me, "Is it really a big step from a work permit by the minister of manpower of a particular province to the day when we are going to need permits to travel across this country? Is it all that far-fetched to think that the next step will be the need for visas to travel from one province to another?" Intelligent and concerned Canadians see this trend toward balkanization. They wonder about it and ask, "What are we going to do about it?" When the Premier of Newfoundland-and I do not want to belabour him-stresses and emphasizes his dilemma, on the one hand, of providing jobs for the people of his province in the flourishing oil industry in Newfoundland, and the problem of denying access to those jobs to Canadians of other provinces, this is not a reassuring situation. The issue, for instance, of owning land anywhere in Canada by Canadians is another problem-

What is proposed, Mr. Speaker? It is proposed that we bring our constitution home, the BNA Act, a further evolution, as I said earlier, a logical transition from a colonial state to a nation. The Governor General is now a Canadian, the new flag which is ours, and the Official Languages Act which reflects the true nature of Canada, and now we are suggesting, after all these years, that we bring the constitution home. With the hon. member's voice one can hear anything he says, but unfortunately he does not make too much sense.
That formula is the only formula that the provincial premiers of this country were able to agree to, and I think that, barring a better one, and with the two-year period in which the provinces and the federal government can get together and come up with a better one, this makes sense.
Let me come back to the other point, Mr. Speaker. What are the entrenched rights which we think Canada needs and which provincial legislation provides in some cases? I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that provincial legislation is only as good as the legislatures or the premiers of that province at that time in history, and there is no guarantee that if our rights are enshrined in provincial legislation, those rights will be found in that same provincial legislation five, ten, or 15 years from now. So our rights must be enshrined in the constitution.
Is anybody here against the enshrinement of the fundamental freedoms, freedom of thought, freedom of religion, freedom of belief, freedom of opinion and expression, freedom of the press and other media, freedom of peaceful assembly and of association?

It is extremely important. How many of my friends in my province, in Quebec when I lived there, refused or had to refuse promotions, transfers by multinational corporations in other provinces, refusing jobs in Ontario, Manitoba or British Columbia because of their unease and concern that their children would not be able to continue their education in French?
